title: No need to hide
hookLine: if you've judged it right, don't hide doing it (Enchiridion 35)

lines: OUT THE SIDE DOOR AT FIVE.
cards: A teenager in a school cafeteria sees the new kid eating alone. She'd like to go sit with him. She'd also like nobody to see her do it.

A man leaves the office at five sharp to coach his daughter's soccer team, and slips out the side door so the others won't notice. People do the right thing, and then do it a little in hiding, as if they've been caught.
Section thirty-five of the Enchiridion is only a few lines long, and it's aimed at exactly that side door.

teach.h: JUDGED RIGHT? DON'T AVOID BEING SEEN.
teach.b: When you've judged that something ought to be done, and you're doing it, Epictetus says, never avoid being seen doing it, even if the many are going to think badly of it. The logic is tidy.

teach.h: WRONG: DON'T. RIGHT: WHY FEAR CRITICS?
teach.b: Either the thing is wrong, or it's right. If it's wrong, don't do it at all. If it's right, the people who'll find fault with it are mistaken, so why be afraid of them?
Hiding a right action quietly hands a vote to people whose opinion, by your own judgment, is wrong. It echoes earlier sections.

Section thirteen asked you to be content to seem foolish about outside things, and section twenty-two warned that anyone who takes up this way of life will be laughed at. Today is the practical follow-through.
You've already accepted that people may think you odd. So stop ducking. There's a test hidden in the sentence, too.

teach.h: THE URGE TO HIDE IS A TEST.
teach.b: If you notice the urge to hide something you're doing, ask why. Sometimes it's only fear of what people will say, and his answer is: then do it in the open.

But sometimes the wish to hide is the first quiet sign that the thing isn't right, and his answer to that is just as plain: then don't do it. This isn't about showing off; the handbook gets to that soon.
It's about not shrinking. A right thing done openly also gives the next person permission to do it too.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes check whether they are hiding a right action out of fear of disapproval, and if so, do it openly; if the wish to hide signals that the act is wrong, they don't do it.

o: the crowd, whose disapproval needn't stop a right act
the wise few whose judgment you should always follow
all the small choices that add up to a life

games.q: no need to hide — tap the pairs.
p: why fear those who find fault?

s: Epictetus says to do good deeds where everyone can admire you
he says don't avoid being seen. that's not showing off; it's not shrinking.
section thirty-five also says: if the act isn't right, don't do it at all
wrong: don't do it. right: why fear those who wrongly find fault?
he says to hide a right action if most people would disapprove
even if the many think badly of it, don't avoid being seen.

games.q: you've decided to leave at five to coach your daughter's team. the office stays late. what does Epictetus say?
o: leave openly. if it's right, why fear those who find fault?
games.why: if you've judged it right, don't avoid being seen. if it were wrong, the answer would be just as plain: don't do it.

practice: Think of one right thing you do a little sheepishly: leaving on time for your family, saying no to a drink, bowing your head before a meal, asking a question in a meeting, sitting with someone others avoid.
Picture yourself doing it in plain view, at an ordinary pace, with no apology and no announcement. Notice whether the urge to hide shows up, and what it's made of.

wordCard.voice: The many. Epictetus' name for the people whose disapproval needn't be feared; if you've judged it right, don't avoid being seen doing it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the many, whose disapproval Enchiridion 35 says not to fear. English borrowed it as hoi polloi.

carryVoice: Your line: without the side door. If it's right, the front door works fine. Day three hundred seventy.
